---
title: "For users"
description: "Everything a player needs: set it up, configure it, and understand just enough of how it works."
---

You have a game whose multiplayer runs on Epic Online Services, and you want it to keep working —
LAN party, couch co-op, or a title whose servers are gone. This section is for you. No SDK
knowledge required; the path is:

1. **[Get the library](building.qmd)** — build the `.so`/`.dll` (or grab a CI artifact), matching
   the *game*, not the machine.
2. **[Drop it in](getting-started.qmd)** — back up Epic's library, put ours in its place, launch.
3. **[Make it yours](configuration.qmd)** — a display name and any tweaks via `eosr.json` or
   `EOSR_*` environment variables.
4. **[Let it through](networking.qmd)** — same LAN, UDP 55789–55798, and the game allowed through
   the firewall.
5. **Play** — host and join from the game's own menus, like it's 2019 and the servers are fine.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Before investing an evening in a specific game, check the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd): the
multiplayer core is real, but voice, achievements, commerce, and anti-cheat are honest stubs
today — the game loads, those features won't function. The
[one-minute census](troubleshooting.qmd#the-game-wont-launch) shows which EOS families a game
touches, no launch required.
:::

## The five rules of the road

If you remember nothing else from this section:

1. **Same LAN, same game, everyone patched.** Discovery is a local broadcast, and the handshake
   refuses a different title or an unpatched copy.
2. **Match the artifact to the game** — a Windows game under Proton still wants the `.dll`.
3. **`profile.key` is your identity.** Back it up; never share it; don't clone it between
   simultaneous machines.
4. **The library never phones home** — not to Epic, not to anyone. If a game needs Epic's
   backend-only features, they're either answered locally or honestly absent.
5. **When in doubt, trace**: `EOSR_TRACE=lifecycle` writes a readable log of everything that
   mattered.
